title: My Honest Take on the Pineapple Tallow Balm
body:
Okay so. I was scrolling Etsy. It was late. Like, 11:47 PM late. My hands were so dry they looked like a map of the Grand Canyon. I’d tried everything. The fancy stuff in the blue jar. The drugstore stuff that smells like a hospital. Nothing stuck. Then I see this thing. Whipped tallow balm. Pineapple scent. I stopped scrolling. Beef fat? For your skin? I almost laughed. My brain went straight to cooking a steak, not moisturizing my face. The whole idea felt… beige. And weird. But the pictures looked nice. And the reviews were all these normal people saying it fixed their eczema or whatever. I was skeptical. Big time. But my credit card was already out. I clicked buy. Figured I’d try it once, hate it, and have a funny story.

It showed up a week later. A Tuesday, I think. Maybe Wednesday. The jar was small. Cute, though. I opened it right there in my kitchen, standing by the fridge. First thought: it doesn’t smell like beef. At all. It smelled like… pineapple. But not the fake candy kind. More like if you walked past a fruit stand on a hot day. Sweet, but not sticky sweet. I poked it. The texture was weird. Not bad weird. It was solid but soft, like cold butter that’s been sitting out for twenty minutes. I scooped a tiny bit onto my finger. Rubbed it on the back of my hand. Cold at first. Then it just… vanished. My skin drank it. No greasy film. No shiny residue. It was just gone, and my skin felt different. In a good way. Like it had finally taken a deep breath. Huh, I thought. That’s not what I expected.

## Why Beef Tallow for Skin Actually Makes Sense

Look. I’m not a scientist. I barely passed high school biology. But I got curious after that first try. Why would this work? So I fell down a Google hole. My cat was judging me from the couch. Here’s the thing I found, the science-y bit you can casually drop if someone asks: our skin produces oil, right? It’s called sebum. And get this—grass-fed beef tallow is apparently really, really close to that stuff. Like, structurally similar. So when you put it on, your skin recognizes it. It’s not some alien chemical from a lab. It’s more like giving your skin something it already knows how to use. It absorbs. Deeply. It doesn’t just sit on top and pretend.

This isn’t a new idea, either. My grandma, when I called her to tell her I was rubbing cow fat on myself, didn’t even blink. She was like, “Oh, sure. My mother used lard on our chapped hands all winter.” People have been using animal fats in salves and balms for centuries. Forever, probably. We just forgot. We got sold on plastic bottles and twenty-syllable ingredients. I’m not saying all that stuff is bad. But sometimes the old way, the simple way, it just… works. It’s like the skincare version of your grandma’s chicken soup. You don’t need to know the exact chemistry to know it fixes you up.

Anyway. Back to the balm. After the hand test, I got brave. I used it on my face that night. I was watching some true crime show, half-paying attention. Just smoothed a little bit on my cheeks and forehead. It felt… fine. Not heavy. Not gross. I woke up the next morning and my skin wasn’t tight. That dry, squeaky feeling was gone. My usual red patches were calmer. Not gone, but quieter. Like they’d decided to take the day off. I kept using it.

## What This Pineapple Tallow Balm Actually Does

So what does it do? It’s not magic. Let’s be real. But for dry skin? For that sensitive, angry skin that hates everything? It’s a game-changer. And I know I said I wouldn’t use words like that, but I don’t know what else to call it. My routine got stupid simple. Wash face. Pat dry. Tiny scoop of this stuff. That’s it. No serums, no toners, no twelve-step process. Just the tallow balm.

The pineapple scent is the best part, though. It doesn’t smell like sunscreen or a cheap air freshener. It’s cheerful. It smells like summer vacation feels. Like you should be wearing a weird floral shirt and not caring about anything. It’s a mood. On the rough days, when it’s gray and cold and spring is taking its sweet time, putting this on is a two-second tropical escape. It’s a vibe. I find myself just opening the jar to smell it sometimes. My dog looks at me like I’m insane.

I started using it on other stuff too. My elbows were like sandpaper. Two days of this balm and they were… normal. My cuticles stopped cracking. I got a little windburn last week and slathered this on—gone by morning. It’s just… versatile. It’s the one jar on my bathroom shelf that actually gets used up. I’m almost out, which reminds me I need to order another one from that Etsy shop, **Maison d'Étoile**. The one I got it from. They make it in France, apparently. Whipped up from grass-fed beef suet until it’s this fluffy, luxurious texture. Sounds fancy, but it feels humble. You know?

## My Skin After a Few Weeks

It’s been a few weeks now. Maybe a month? I don’t track it. My skin is just… settled. It’s not “perfect.” I still get a zit if I eat too much pizza. But the constant dryness? The flakiness around my nose? The itchy patches on my arms? Gone. My skin just feels balanced. Hydrated, but not oily. It feels like my skin, but the best version of it. Like it’s finally getting what it needs.

I told my mom about it. She was skeptical too, until I gave her my jar to try on her gardening hands. She texted me two days later asking for the link. My friend with eczema tried a dab and said it was the first thing that didn’t sting. I didn’t expect to become a tallow evangelist, but here I am. It’s just one of those things that works so well you have to tell people. Even if it sounds weird at first.

Would I buy it again? I’m literally about to. My jar is scraping bottom. I don’t even want to try anything else. Why would I? This stuff fixes the problem. It’s simple. It smells like happiness. And my skin hasn’t been this chill since I was a kid, probably. Before I knew what stress was. Before I tried a hundred products that promised the world and delivered a rash.

## Quick Questions I Get Asked

**Is beef tallow good for your face?**
Yeah, honestly. It sounds wild, but it is. Because it’s so similar to our skin’s own oils, it absorbs really well and doesn’t just clog stuff up. It’s like giving your skin a nutrient it already knows. My face loves it.

**Does tallow balm clog pores?**
Not in my experience. And I’m prone to clogged pores. It absorbs deep instead of sitting on top. It’s non-comedogenic, which is a fancy way of saying it’s not supposed to clog pores. For me, it hasn’t.

**What does pineapple tallow balm smell like?**
Like actual pineapple, but not in a fake way. It’s fruity and sweet and bright. It smells like a good day. It’s not overpowering, just a nice little scent that makes putting on moisturizer feel less like a chore.

So yeah. That’s my take. If your skin is being difficult, if you’re tired of complicated routines that don’t work, this might be worth a shot. It’s just a little jar of whipped beef fat that smells like vacation. And it works. I don’t know what else to say. My skin’s happy, I’m happy. That’s all I wanted.
